To a suspension of methyltriphenylphosphonium bromide (18 mmol, 1.2 equiv.) in anhydrous THF (50 mL) was added potassium tert-butoxide (21 mmol, 1.4 equiv.). After stirring the reaction mixture at room temperature for 30 min, the corresponding aldehyde (15 mmol, 1.0 equiv.) was added. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 16 h, diluted with pentane (20 mL). The mixture was filtered through a silica gel plug, eluting with pentane, and the resulting filtrate concentrated in vacuo. The residue was purified by chromatography on silica gel, eluting with pentane, to give the corresponding 1,3-dienes.<sup>[6]</sup>

We have calculated and plotted the spin density distributions for the two key allylic radical intermediates, Int2-a and Int2-b, derived from 1,3-butadiene. As shown in Figure S3, the spin density in Int2-a is primarily localized on the terminal carbon atom (C4), with a calculated population of 0.75, compared to a value of 0.71 at the C2 position. This indicates tendency for sulfur dioxide addition at the 4-position, favoring the 1,4-addition pathway over the sterically more hindered or electronically less favorable 1,2-addition. A similar spin density distribution pattern is observed for intermediate Int2-b, where the terminal carbon also shows a higher spin population (0.74) than the internal C2 position (0.72). Spin density populations were evaluated with Multiwfn<sup>[21]</sup>, and the pictures of spin density populations were prepared with VMD<sup>[22]</sup>.

Polyfluoroarylsulfones represent an important class of compounds with broad applications in pharmaceutical chemistry and materials science, yet their eficient and selective synthesis remains challenging. Herein, we report a visible-light-driven, photoredox-catalyzed cascade reaction that enables simultaneous difluoromethylation, sulfur dioxide reintegration, and polyfluoroarylation of conjugated dienes using sodium difluoromethanesulfinate ( \mathsf { C F } _ { 2 } \mathsf { H S O } _ { 2 } \mathsf { N a } ) as a bifunctional reagent. This strategy leverages the dual role of \mathsf { C F } _ { 2 } \mathsf { H S O } _ { 2 } \mathsf { N a } . which acts as both a source of { \mathsf { C F } } _ { 2 } { \mathsf { H } } radicals and an in situ { \mathsf { S O } } _ { 2 } surrogate, facilitating the atom-economical construction of polyfluoroaryl-substituted allylic sulfones under exceptionally mild conditions. The reaction proceeds with high regio- and stereoselectivity, afording either 1,4- or 1,2-addition products depending on the diene substrate. Notably, the method is applicable to commodity chemicals such as 1,3-butadiene and enables late-stage functionalization of complex polyfluoroarenes. Mechanistic studies and DFT calculations provide insight into the reaction pathway, including the unprecedented trapping of a delocalized allylic radical by { \mathsf { S O } } _ { 2 } and the origin of selectivity. This work ofers a practical, modular, and sustainable approach to accessing structurally diverse polyfluoroarylsulfones, with potential utility in synthetic and medicinal chemistry.

In our investigation of the radical difluoromethylation/SO reincorporation/polyfluoroarylation cascade reaction, model substrates ^ { 1 , 3 \cdot } -butadiene (1a), \mathrm { C F } _ { 2 } \mathrm { H S O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { N a } (2a), and methyl pentafluorobenzoate (3a) were employed. The reaction was carried out using 4-CzIPN as the photocatalyst (PC), \mathbf { Z } \mathbf { n } \mathbf { C l } _ { 2 } as an additive, and DMSO as the solvent under irradiation with 5 W blue LEDs for 48 h. Pleasingly, the desired ^ { 1 , 4 \cdot } -difluoromethylation/sulfonylation product 4aa was obtained in an excellent yield of 86% with an E / Z selectivity of 6 . 2 : 1 . The addition of inorganic bases such as { \bf K } _ { 3 } { \bf P } { \bf O } _ { 4 } and \mathbf { K } _ { 2 } \mathbf { C O } _ { 3 } improved the E/Z selectivity, albeit with a slight reduction in yield. Notably, when \mathrm { N a } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C O } _ { 3 } was used as the base, the target product 4aa (CCDC 2350968)<sup>21</sup> was obtained in 74% yield along with 4aa′ (7%). In contrast, the use of \mathrm { C s } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C O } _ { 3 } resulted in decreased selectivity and eficiency. Organic bases such as DABCO proved inefective for this transformation. Screening of photocatalysts showed that an organic photocatalyst (PC-2) efectively promoted the reaction, delivering 4aa (79%) and 4aa′ (13%) with slightly lower E / Z selectivity. Conversely, Ru- or Ir-based complexes (PC-3 to PC-5) proved suboptimal, leading to diminished yields. Solvents such as DMF and DMAc aforded the product with moderately reduced yields and selectivity, whereas \mathrm { C H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { C N } , THF, and DCM did not yield the desired product. Based on these results, the conditions in the equation shown in Table 1 were selected as optimal and identified as the standard conditions for further substrate scope investigations.

Furthermore, phenyl-substituted 1,3-dienes were found to undergo the radical difluoromethylation / { \bf S } { \bf O } _ { 2 } reintegration/ polyfluoroarylation cascade under slightly modified conditions, yielding 1,2-addition products with specific stereoselectivity. We subsequently explored the substrate scope of this 1,2-addition system. As shown in Scheme 2D, 1,3-dienes featuring electron-donating groups (methyl, tert-butyl, phenyl, methoxy) or halogen (fluorine) groups at the para-position of the aryl ring readily underwent the cascade reaction, providing the desired products 5ca–5ga in moderate to good yields (40–77%). The scope extended to substituted ^ { 1 , 3 \cdot } -dienes featuring a range of aryl substituents, from the strong electron-withdrawing \mathrm { C F } _ { 3 } group (5ha, 51%) to electron-donating methoxy (5ia, 52%), methyl (5ja, 42%), and ethyl (5ka, 74%; CCDC 2350968)<sup>21</sup> groups at either meta or ortho positions, all of which proceeded smoothly. Substrates bearing 3,5-dimethyl substituents (5la, 85%) as well as heterocyclic systems such as benzofuran (5ma, 57%) also proved suitable for the transformation.

Mechanistic investigations were carried out to elucidate the potential reaction pathways. Control experiments demonstrated that both visible-light irradiation and the photoredox catalyst are indispensable for the formation of compound 4aa (Scheme 3A). When TEMPO (3.0 equiv.) was added as a radical inhibitor, the formation of 4aa was completely suppressed, and the TEMPO-adducted difluoromethyl radical species 6a was detected by GC-MS (Scheme 3B). The use of the cyclopropane-containing styrene derivative 7a as a radical clock aforded the ring-opening product 6b in 49% yield. Similarly, when a 1,6-diene was employed as the substrate, the radical cyclization product 6c was obtained in 68% yield (Scheme 3C). These results suggest the involvement of a difluoromethyl radical species in the reaction system and indicate that the addition of the difluoromethyl group to the alkene proceeds via a radical pathway. Furthermore, a two-step experiment was designed to evaluate the potential formation of a difluoromethylation/sulfonylation intermediate derived from 1,3-butadiene (1a). As illustrated in Scheme 3D, a mixture of 1a and 2 was first subjected to blue LED irradiation in the presence of 4-CzIPN as the photocatalyst for 24 hours. Compound 3a was then added, and the reaction was continued for an additional 24 hours in the dark. Notably, 4aa was isolated in 46% yield, supporting the putative involvement of a difluoromethylation/ sulfonylation intermediate, tentatively assigned as sulfinate salt 6d. The formation of this intermediate was further corroborated by HRMS analysis of the reaction mixture. To further verify the accumulation of sulfinate in the reaction system, benzyl bromide was added to the mixture after 24 h of reaction. The system was then allowed to react for an additional 24 h under dark conditions. This process yielded 4aa and 4aa′ with a combined 71% yield, and notably, a small amount of the 4at was also isolated. The generation of 4at confirms the accumulation of a sulfinate salt intermediate 6d in the system, indicating that the nucleophilic substitution between the sulfinate and the polyfluoroarene constitutes the rate-determining step of the reaction. The comparable outcomes observed for the mixed E/Z (Scheme 3E) and pure trans conjugated alkenes —both in terms of yield and stereochemistry—corroborate the delocalized nature of the allylic radical intermediate. This delocalization enables rapid isomerization, efectively interconverting the cis and trans configurations. Fluorescence quenching experiments revealed that the excited-state photocatalyst is more efectively quenched by sodium difluoromethanesulfinate than by polyfluoroarenes or conjugated dienes (Fig. S1). This observation, combined with the redox potentials of the \mathrm { C F } _ { 2 } \mathrm { H S O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { N a } \left( E _ { \mathrm { o x } } \ : = \ : 0 . 5 9 \ : \mathrm { ~ V ~ } \right. vs. \mathbf { S C E } ) ^ { 1 3 i } and the photocatalyst \left( E _ { 1 / 2 } ^ { \mathrm { P C * / P C - } } ~ = ~ \mathrm { \stackrel { . } { 1 . 3 8 } ~ V } \right. vs. SCE),<sup>18h</sup> supports a reductive quenching mechanism. To clarify the role of \mathbf { Z n C l } _ { 2 } , several control experiments were performed. First, mixing \mathrm { Z n C l } _ { 2 } with sodium difluoromethanesulfinate produced new signals in both ^ 1 \mathrm { H } and { } ^ { 1 9 } \mathrm { F } NMR spectra, indicating the formation of a new fluoroalkyl sulfinate species. When \mathrm { Z n } ( \mathbf { S O } _ { 2 } \mathbf { C F } _ { 2 } \mathbf { H } ) _ { 2 } was used directly, the target product was obtained in 43% yield. In contrast, only 36% yield was achieved in the absence of ZnCl . These results suggest that ion exchange occurs between sodium fluoroalkylsulfinate and ZnCl to generate a reactive fluoroalkyl–metal intermediate, which facilitates the transformation.

Based on these experimental results and the previous literature, a plausible catalytic cycle for the 1,4-difluoromethylative sulfonylation reaction is proposed in Scheme 3F. The cycle begins with blue LED irradiation generating the excited-state photocatalyst 4-CzIPN*, which undergoes reductive quenching with \mathrm { C F } _ { 2 } \mathrm { H S O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { N a } . This process releases \mathrm { { S O } } _ { 2 } and generates the 4 { \cdot } \mathrm { C z I P N } ^ { \bullet - } along with a \mathrm { C F } _ { 2 } \mathrm { H } radical. The \mathrm { C F } _ { 2 } \mathrm { H } radical adds to 1,3-diene (1a), forming an allylic radical intermediate B. This radical is subsequently trapped by \mathrm { { S O } } _ { 2 } at the terminal position, yielding sulfonyl radical C, which is then reduced by the 4 { \cdot } \mathrm { C z I P N } ^ { \bullet - } to form sulfonyl anion D. Finally, intermediate D undergoes nucleophilic aromatic substitution ( { \mathsf { S } } _ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathsf { A r } } ) with a polyfluoroarene via C–F bond cleavage, delivering the desired cascade product 4 and completing the catalytic cycle.

However, certain issues regarding site selectivity and Z/E selectivity in this reaction require further clarification. To address these questions, we employed DFT calculations to gain deeper mechanistic insights (Scheme 3G). Computational results reveal that the difluoromethyl radical, generated from the desulfonation of the difluoromethanesulfinate radical, undergoes transformation via transition state TS1 \begin{array} { l } { { \left( \Delta G ^ { \ddagger } \ \right. \ = } } \end{array} 7.6 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup>) to form intermediate Int2-a. This intermediate can isomerize to yield Int2-b. The subsequent addition of \mathrm { { S O } } _ { 2 } to Int2-a exhibits notable site-selectivity: the Gibbs free energy barrier for the ^ { 1 , 4 } -addition transition state TS2-a \begin{array} { l } { { \left( \Delta G ^ { \ddagger } \ \right. \ = } } \end{array} 3.2 kcal \mathbf { m o l } ^ { - 1 } ) is 4.4 kcal \mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } } lower than that of the ^ { 1 , 2 \mathrm { - } } addition transition state TS2-c \left( \Delta G ^ { \ddagger } \ = \ 7 . 6 \right. kcal \mathbf { m o l } ^ { - 1 } ) . This thermodynamically favored pathway is consistent with the experimental observation that no 1,2-addition byproduct was detected. The spin density distribution of intermediate Int2-a was computed. As shown in Fig. S3 ( \mathrm { S I } ) , the spin population is _ { 0 . 7 5 } at the 4-position, which is slightly higher than the value of 0.71 at the 2-position. Further evaluation of steric efects indicated that the barrier for the 1,4-addition transition state TS2b \left( \Delta G ^ { \ddagger } = 4 . 5 \right. kcal mol<sup>−1</sup>), derived from the cis-configured intermediate Int2b, is 1.3 kcal \mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } } (corresponding to 90 : 10 E/Z at 25 °C), which is higher than that of the preferred transconfigured TS2a, aligning with the experimentally observed stereoselectivity. The reduction of the sulfonyl radical by the photocatalyst to form the sulfonyl anion is highly exothermic, thereby facilitating rapid conversion of the unstable allylic sulfonyl radical and promoting the eficient coupling between the delocalized allylic radical and { \bf S } { \bf O } _ { 2 } { - \bf a } previously unreported transformation. The resulting sulfonyl anion subsequently undergoes defluorination via a five-membered cyclic transition state TS3 \left( \Delta G ^ { \ddagger } = 2 1 . 7 \right. kcal \mathbf { m o l } ^ { - 1 } ) in the presence of a metal cation such as { { \bf { N } } { \bf { a } } ^ { + } } , leading to the final product 4aa. Furthermore, since reactions involving 1-phenyl-1,3-diene exclusively yield 1,2-addition products, we conducted additional theoretical calculations (Scheme 3H). Our analysis reveals a 3.1 kcal \mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } lower energy barrier for the 1,2- addition transition state (TS2d) compared to its 1,4-addition counterpart (TS2e). This kinetic preference is rationalized by distortion/interaction analysis, which examines the distortion energies of the alkyl radical and \mathbf { S O } _ { 2 } and their interaction energies. The key finding, from Scheme ^ { 3 \mathrm { I } , } is the substantially larger distortion energy required for the alkyl radical in the 1,4-addition process (8.5 vs. 5.8 kcal \mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } ) . This increased distortion energy accounts for the higher activation barrier, thereby confirming the thermodynamic favorability of the ^ { 1 , 2 \mathrm { - } } addition.

visual_inspections.description: Table 1 drawing shows butadiene, the methyl-pentafluorobenzoate starting graph and the E/Z 1,4 sulfone product pair. Product configuration was additionally viewed in the enlarged private table crop. Source labels are not exported.

Scheme 2 shows para-aryl sulfone connectivity, the butadiene product and a separate terminal-aryl-diene 1,2 product class. The unsubstituted phenyl product is drawn as Ph-CH=CH-CH(SO2Ar)-CH2-CHF2, with a 74% yield. Caption distinguishes DMSO/base/5 W butadiene conditions from DMF/no-base/40 W phenyl conditions.

Scheme 3 includes the proposed radical/sulfinate photocycle, the connected butadiene free-energy profile with fragmentation, initial addition, alternative SO2 captures, catalyst reduction and Na-assisted SNAr; a TS3 structure; and the phenyl TS/distortion panel. The panel was enlarged privately to read 5.8/8.5 radical distortion, 0.6/0.8 SO2 distortion, 5.9/6.2 interaction magnitudes and distinct Delta E versus Delta Delta G labels.

Body text distinguishes experimental controls/cycle interpretation from DFT results, and reports local capture barriers, the E/Z estimate, reduction, sodium-associated substitution and phenyl comparison. No whole page is exported.
Conclusions and author contributions are visible; the contributions explicitly attribute DFT to K. J. and L. Z.

Table S3 depicts the E/Z butadiene products with 74%/7% in DMSO. Table S4 depicts the unsubstituted terminal-phenyl diene/product and highlights 4CzIPN in DMF giving 74%, without added carbonate in the selected row; the footnote gives 40 W blue LEDs and quantities.

Starting-material table depicts the unsubstituted terminal-phenyl E diene and the methyl 2,3,4,5,6-pentafluorobenzoate graph; the methylenation preparation is consistent with that terminal diene connectivity.

Product drawing and named characterization establish the E butadiene para-aryl sulfone, the methyl ester, terminal CHF2 and the reported 74% isolated yield. Nearby trifluoromethyl analog is a different experimental entry and is not substituted into this task.

Product drawing and characterization establish the unsubstituted phenyl E alkene, sulfur at the adjacent chain carbon, terminal CHF2, para-aryl methyl-ester connectivity and 74% yield; no absolute configuration is assigned.

Method text, both spin-density maps and the sulfinate-radical coordinates are visible. The maps show the stated terminal/internal populations; the radical precursor retains CHF2 bonded to sulfur and two oxygens.

SO2, difluoromethyl radical, butadiene and initial-addition coordinate/energy records are visible. The butadiene coordinates correspond to an unbranched four-carbon diene with two terminal methylenes.

Original page ordering separates preceding TS1 continuation from Int2-a/Int2-b and TS2-a. The two allylic records retain the same five-carbon CHF2-ended skeleton; table extraction labels do not define atom identities by themselves.
The neutral 4CzIPN heading and its coordinate list begin after the reduced-state continuation. The central-ring carbon/nitrile geometry is visible and was used only for private identity checking.
Neutral-photocatalyst coordinate continuation shows carbon, hydrogen and carbazolyl nitrogen records; no research calculation was executed.

The neutral-photocatalyst coordinates end before the TS3-pre heading. Together with pages 36-37 the record has C56H32N6, two meta nitriles and four tricoordinate nitrogen attachments, consistent with 4CzIPN.
The 4aa heading follows the TS3 continuation. Its aryl coordinates locate ester and sulfur para on the ring and include an extra sodium/fluoride model context continued on the next page.

Organic-product chain/NaF continuation appears ABOVE the actual TS2-d heading. The original page therefore resolves the extracted row that wrongly leads with TS2-d before those preceding coordinates. The TS2-d list starts below its DMF energy header.

TS2-d continuation ends above TS2-e; TS2-e has explicit DMF energies and the same terminal-phenyl, CHF2-ended carbon backbone. The competing structures differ in allylic bond localization and sulfur contact: 1,2 capture retains the phenyl-side alkene, whereas 1,4 capture shifts localization toward the internal diene bond. The starting E assignment is independently supported by the precursor drawing, not imposed on both TS structures.
Independently viewed the original general-information page: all reactions under nitrogen and butadiene supplied as a 2 mol/L THF solution.
Independently viewed the original reaction procedure and E/Z product drawing: 500 microlitres of butadiene stock, 1.5 mL dry DMSO and the stated reagent/additive quantities.

Independently viewed the solution-phase 4CzIPN emission/quenching experiment. It supports dissolved molecular photocatalysis, not complete dissolution of every inorganic additive at preparative loading.
Independently viewed the original title, DOI and publication date; these remain private provenance rather than autonomous solver inputs.
Independently viewed the TS2-a continuation and TS2-b/TS2-c records; the source contains actual coordinate and thermochemistry records beyond the asset captions.
Independently viewed the reduced 4CzIPN coordinate/energy record underlying the bound asset caption; the caption alone is not treated as scientific evidence.
Independently viewed the Na-associated substitution precomplex continuation and TS3 record in the connected formation investigation.

public_identity_provenance.derivation: Adds the graph-explicit four-carbon conjugated diene identity, verified against the original 1a coordinate record and starting/product drawings; this is not an optimized starting geometry.

Clarifies the salt molecular graph and CHF2 hydrogen/fluorine count without disclosing fragmentation, radicals or the reagent dual-role interpretation. The computed radical precursor has the same covalent skeleton; the experimental identity supplies the sodium salt state.

Expands the unambiguous starting arene name to locants and a graph description. The starting-material drawing and experimental procedure identify a methyl ester, not another pentafluoroarene; the computed aryl-product record has sulfur para to this ester.

Retains all Stage05 butadiene conditions and makes their quantities explicit. Establishes the actually used related phenyl-comparison conditions (DMF, 40 W blue LEDs, no added carbonate) rather than silently applying the butadiene DMSO/base conditions to the second system. Also resolves the photocatalyst molecular identity from its neutral coordinate record. These are observed conditions/identities, not an author computation recipe. The original general-information page specifies a 2 mol/L THF butadiene stock and the product procedure doses 500 microlitres of that stock into 1.5 mL DMSO. Preserve this neutral experimental solvent context instead of silently treating the primary-solvent label as neat DMSO; the reported continuum model remains a distinct conditional reference.

Replaces source product labels with verified ordinary product graphs and alkene identities while preserving the 74%/7% isolated yields. Makes the observed absence of a detected 1,2 product explicit without inventing a detection limit or a rate ratio. The published organic E-product graph agrees with the original computed product, whose coordinate model also includes NaF; no computed geometry or model spectator is exposed.

Resolves vague phenyl-substituted diene wording to the unsubstituted terminal-phenyl E diene actually represented by the computed TS2-d/TS2-e graphs and representative experimental precursor/product. Both transition-state records contain C11H11F2SO2 with CHF2 at one end and phenyl at the other, not an internal-phenyl isomer. Original PDF page ordering, rather than the misplaced extracted TS2-d heading, resolves the continuation rows. The E starting configuration is established independently by the original precursor drawing, not by imposing an unchanged phenyl-side alkene on both capture transition structures; their allylic bond localization differs while their terminal-phenyl carbon backbone agrees.

Makes the existing same-system phenyl observation usable by identifying the representative product graph and E alkene, supplying its observed 74% yield, and stating the absence of a numerical detection-limit/enantioselectivity input. Does not extend scoring to the uncomputed substituted-aryl experimental library or predict a source-unspecified absolute configuration.
